strengths: The core idea—using coarse 3D primitives (cuboids/ellipsoids) plus rasterized ground surfaces as the foundational representation for *generative* large-scale 3D urban scene modeling—is novel and well-motivated. The paper convincingly argues why primitives are better suited than voxel grids for memory efficiency, compositionality, and editability, and it is (to my knowledge) the first to formulate generative scene synthesis in this representation.

The hybrid and disentangled latent design is technically clean and demonstrably useful. Splitting the joint latent into ground and object channel groups (Sec. 3.2) is validated by the ablation (Fig. 4a), and it directly enables non-trivial downstream applications without fine-tuning: inpainting, outpainting, and ground-conditioned object generation (Fig. 12). This is a meaningful practical contribution beyond a single reconstruction benchmark.

The Cholesky-based 6D parameterization of object orientation+size (Sec. B.1) is a principled fix for quaternion sign ambiguity. The mathematical justification (sign-invariance of the scatter matrix, symmetry, positive-definiteness) is correct, and the empirical comparison (Fig. 4b) shows clear and consistent gains over quaternion encoding across training-set sizes—a rare case of a small representational change being rigorously validated.

The memory/quality tradeoff is well characterized: 2.52 MB/scene vs. 8.00 MB for the voxel baseline at 256²×32, with comparable reconstruction IoU and substantially better generative metrics (FID 55 vs 156, Precision 0.45 vs 0.03). The efficiency argument is concrete and reproducible.

The paper is clearly written, the figures (especially the overview Fig. 2 and the qualitative comparisons in Figs. 5–8) are informative, the ablation suite is thoughtful (latent split, joint vs. separate training, Cholesky vs. quaternion), and the supplementary material is thorough (losses, weights, architectures, dataset construction, and an honest limitations/failure-case section).

The generative results are backed by more than a single metric: the paper reports Precision/Recall/FID/IS, includes a sensitivity analysis of the P/R evaluation to sampling strategy and neighborhood size (Fig. 9), and shows controllability (vegetation-density conditioning in Fig. 11).
weaknesses: The experimental comparison is narrow: a single baseline (SemCity) on a single dataset (KITTI-360). While the paper justifies this (KITTI-360 is the only dense primitive-annotated outdoor dataset), the absence of comparisons to other recent 3D/2.5D scene generation methods (e.g., CityDreamer, SceneControl, hierarchical voxel methods) makes it hard to situate the contribution relative to the broader literature.

The reconstruction claim is framed generously. In Fig. 3a, SemCity at 256²×32† (1M queries) reaches 97.69 IoU / 93.81 mIoU versus PrITTI's 90.58 / 70.27. The paper calls this "comparable reconstruction quality," but the mIoU gap (70 vs 94) is substantial. The efficiency gain is real, but the text should more explicitly acknowledge that the voxel baseline is more accurate at its highest-fidelity setting, and that the tradeoff is memory-for-fidelity rather than strict parity.

The generative metrics are partly self-defined. Precision/Recall depend on a custom minimum-distance sampling strategy and neighborhood size k (Sec. 4.2 and Sec. D), and FID is computed on 2D top-down semantic renderings rather than on 3D structure. This weakens cross-paper comparability and means the reported FID gap (55 vs 156) may partly reflect representation/renderer differences rather than pure generation quality.

The "resolution-independent" framing is only partly accurate. Object primitives are resolution-independent, but ground surfaces are rasterized into 256² height/occupancy maps and extruded (Sec. 3.1, B.2.4). Ground geometry is therefore bounded by the raster resolution, which the paper itself notes as a limitation (Sec. E) but does not reconcile with the abstract's stronger claim.

The photo-realistic street-view synthesis (Fig. 8) relies on an off-the-shelf ControlNet trained on KITTI-360; it is an application demonstration rather than a methodological contribution, and the manuscript does not quantify its fidelity (no FID/PSNR/user study), so its inclusion adds little evidentiary weight.

No perceptual or user study is provided for the generated 3D scenes or the edits; the evaluation of controllability/editability is largely qualitative (Figs. 6, 12), so the "editable" claim rests mostly on illustrative examples.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and novel representation for 3D semantic scene generation, replacing memory-heavy voxel grids with compact, editable object primitives (cuboids/ellipsoids) plus rasterized ground surfaces. This is a genuinely new formulation for the large-scale urban scene generation task, and the paper convincingly argues why primitives are better suited for memory efficiency, compositionality, and localized edits.

The memory-efficiency claim is well-supported: PrITTI uses 2.52 MB per scene versus SemCity's 8.00 MB (over 3× reduction) while retaining competitive reconstruction quality. This is a concrete, practically meaningful advantage that supports the central motivation.

Generative results are substantially stronger than the voxel-based baseline: FID 55.04 vs. 156.24, Precision 0.4532 vs. 0.0288, and Recall 0.436 vs. 0.0472, with an extensive supporting figure (Fig. 5, Fig. 11) showing clearer object boundaries and more structured layouts.

The disentangled latent structure (separate ground and object channels) is a clean design choice that enables several downstream applications—inpainting, outpainting, ground-conditioned object generation, and object-level translation/rotation/scaling—without any fine-tuning. This is a strong practical demonstration that follows naturally from the representation.

The Cholesky-based joint encoding of orientation and size is technically elegant and well-justified: the sign-invariance and positive-definiteness arguments (Sec. B.1) are correct, and the synthetic ablation (Fig. 4b) shows it consistently outperforms quaternion parameterization, especially as data scales.

The paper is clearly written, with informative overview figures (Fig. 1, 2) and a thorough supplementary that documents dataset construction, loss weighting, architecture, and training details, supporting reproducibility.
The ablations (latent split, joint vs. separate training, Cholesky vs. quaternion) are thoughtfully designed and directly test the key design decisions.
weaknesses: The evaluation breadth is narrow: only one dataset (KITTI-360) and one baseline (SemCity). The paper acknowledges the dataset limitation, but a stronger case would require additional comparisons or at least a broader qualitative comparison to related voxel/layout methods (e.g., XCube, CityDreamer).

The reconstruction comparison is somewhat unfavorable on its own terms: PrITTI reports IoU 90.58 / mIoU 70.27, while the upsampled SemCity baseline reaches 97.69 / 93.81. The paper argues this is due to voxelization approximation error for evaluation and that the representation is inherently resolution-independent, which is a fair caveat, but it means the reconstruction-quality evidence is weaker than the generation-quality evidence.

Generation quality is measured only through 2D orthographic semantic-map projections (FID/Precision/Recall/IS), not through native 3D metrics. While this follows prior practice, it is an indirect proxy and does not fully validate the 3D geometric plausibility of the generated primitives.

The 'first primitive-based formulation' claim is somewhat strong given prior primitive/box-based driving-scene work (e.g., SceneControl, SLEDGE); the distinction (richer primitive types, arbitrary ground polygons, semantic classes) is argued but the novelty framing could be more carefully qualified.

Ground surfaces are represented via rasters extruded into 3D, which inherits the 256² resolution limit and produces coarse ground geometry; the paper acknowledges this, but it partially undercuts the resolution-independence argument made for the representation.

Some failure modes (floating/disconnected objects, poor outpainting with empty conditioning regions) are shown only qualitatively in the supplement; a more quantitative characterization of when the method fails would strengthen the analysis.

strengths: The paper proposes a compact hybrid primitive-based representation for urban 3D semantic scene generation, combining rasterized ground maps with vectorized object primitives. This is a sensible and practically useful representation for memory efficiency and local editability.

The disentangled latent design and the Cholesky-based encoding of object size and orientation are technically interesting. The Cholesky parameterization is motivated well and is supported by an ablation, albeit on synthetic data.
The method is clearly described and the supplementary material provides extensive implementation details, including architecture, losses, and training configurations, which improves reproducibility.
The downstream applications, especially inpainting, outpainting, and primitive-level editing, illustrate the potential of the representation and are qualitatively compelling.
weaknesses: The generation comparison against SemCity is not convincing. PrITTI is conditioned on vegetation-density labels, while the SemCity baseline appears to be evaluated without an equivalent conditioning mechanism. In addition, SemCity is trained for only 18 epochs versus 300 epochs for PrITTI. The near-zero precision/recall for SemCity therefore likely reflects an unfair training/conditioning setup rather than a true representational gap.

The reconstruction claim is overstated. At the highest reported SemCity configuration, SemCity achieves mIoU 93.81 and IoU 97.69, whereas PrITTI reports mIoU 70.27 and IoU 90.58. Calling this 'competitive' or 'comparable' reconstruction quality is not supported by the numbers. The memory advantage is real, but it is a trade-off, not evidence of superior or comparable quality.

The central controllability and editability claims are supported only qualitatively. Inpainting, outpainting, object-level editing, and photo-realistic street-view synthesis are shown in figures but have no quantitative evaluation, no user study, and no systematic comparison against baselines. For a paper whose main selling point is controllable/editable generation, this is a major evidentiary gap.

The Cholesky-versus-quaternion ablation is conducted only on synthetic single-vehicle data with random scale and yaw. This does not establish that the proposed parameterization is beneficial for full urban scene layouts with multiple categories and complex interactions.

The novelty is incremental: the framework combines standard components such as a VAE, DiT latent diffusion, DETR-style object queries, RePaint-style latent manipulation, and an existing Cholesky factorization idea. The claim of being the 'first' primitive-based formulation for large-scale 3D urban scene generation is also overbroad given prior primitive-based and compositional 3D scene generation work.

Evaluation is limited to KITTI-360 with a 64m x 64m field of view and static scenes. There is no cross-dataset validation, no evaluation of scalability to larger or more diverse urban environments, and no quantitative analysis of failure cases beyond the supplement's qualitative examples.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated primitive-based representation for large-scale 3D urban semantic scene generation, replacing memory-inefficient voxel grids with compact and directly editable object primitives and rasterized ground surfaces.
Proposes a novel latent VAE with disentangled ground/object branches and a Cholesky-based parameterization for 6D object orientation/size, improving stability compared with quaternion encodings.
Provides extensive experiments on KITTI-360, including reconstruction, generation, ablations, and qualitative comparisons against voxel-based baselines such as SemCity, PDD, and XCube.

Reported generative metrics (precision, recall, FID, IS) and inference speed/memory comparisons are strong relative to baselines, and downstream scene editing, inpainting, outpainting, object-level editing, and photo-realistic view synthesis demonstrate practical usefulness.

The paper is generally clear, well-organized, and makes a convincing case for primitive-based representations in urban scene generation, with relevance to autonomous driving simulation and virtual world modeling.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to KITTI-360 with a custom train/test split, so broader generalization to other urban datasets or scene types is not demonstrated.

Comparison fairness is a concern: PrITTI is evaluated with class-balanced conditioning for vegetation density, while baseline methods are unconditional and less tuned for this voxelized setup; some baseline results may therefore be pessimistic.

The reconstruction results on standard voxel metrics in Table 1 show PrITTI's voxelized version below optimized baselines like SemCity-1M and XCube, making the "state-of-the-art reconstruction quality" claim somewhat nuanced.

Reproducibility is weakened by the abstract stating code/models are available at a missing/blank URL, and by the heavy training pipeline requiring multiple A100 GPU-days plus non-trivial dataset preprocessing.

The fixed-size-per-category primitive prediction with 95th-percentile capacity thresholds and farthest-discarding may limit performance in dense scenes, and the primitive representation fundamentally struggles with fine-grained attachments such as lamps and fences, as acknowledged by the authors.
Downstream applications are mainly demonstrated qualitatively; there is little quantitative or task-based evaluation of inpainting/outpainting, editing, or photo-realistic synthesis quality.

The method is only compared against voxel-based baselines; other recent 3D generative approaches, including neural-field or other primitive-based methods, are not quantitatively benchmarked, limiting the scope of the state-of-the-art claim.

strengths: Introduces a novel primitive-based representation for 3D semantic urban scene generation, effectively addressing the memory, resolution, and editability limitations of voxel-based methods.

Proposes a disentangled latent representation that separates ground and object channels, enabling controllable manipulation such as inpainting, outpainting, and object-level editing without additional fine-tuning.

Employs a Cholesky-based parameterization for object orientation and size, which provides better numerical stability and avoids sign ambiguity compared to quaternion encodings, as demonstrated through ablation studies.

Achieves competitive reconstruction quality (IoU, mIoU) and superior generation quality (FID, IS, Precision/Recall) compared to strong voxel-based baselines (SemCity, PDD, XCube) on the KITTI-360 dataset, while being significantly faster and more memory-efficient.

Extensive experiments validate the method across reconstruction, generation, and multiple downstream applications, with thorough quantitative and qualitative results, including failure cases and limitations.
The paper is well-written, clearly structured, and provides sufficient implementation details and supplementary material for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The object representation is limited to coarse primitives (cuboids and ellipsoids), which restricts geometric fidelity and may not capture fine details such as lamps, fences, or complex vehicle shapes, as acknowledged by the authors.
The method relies on datasets that provide dense primitive-level annotations (e.g., KITTI-360), which are scarce, limiting its applicability to domains where such annotations are unavailable.
Controllability in the diffusion model is demonstrated only for vegetation density; extension to other attributes or fine-grained object placement is not quantitatively evaluated.

The photo-realistic street-view synthesis is an application that uses an external ControlNet model fine-tuned on KITTI-360, so it is not a core contribution and its quality depends on the downstream model.
The evaluation is conducted only on KITTI-360; while this is the standard dataset for this task, broader evaluation on other urban datasets would strengthen the claims of generality.
No user study or perceptual evaluation is provided to complement the quantitative metrics, which could further validate the visual quality and editability of the generated scenes.

strengths: The paper proposes a compact and intuitive primitive-based representation for urban 3D scene layout generation, moving beyond dense voxel grids and enabling object-level manipulation.

The hybrid design of rasterized ground surfaces plus vectorized object primitives is technically coherent, and the disentangled latent space for ground and objects is a sensible way to support downstream editing tasks.
The Cholesky-based parameterization for object orientation and size is a clean modification over quaternion encodings; the ablation in Fig. 4 supports its practical benefit.

The method achieves strong quantitative generation results on KITTI-360 in terms of Precision, Recall, FID, and inference time compared with the evaluated voxel-based baselines, and it yields qualitatively diverse scenes.
The paper is generally well written, with substantial supplementary material covering dataset construction, architecture details, and additional qualitative results.
Downstream applications such as inpainting, outpainting, object editing, and view synthesis are demonstrated, and the code/models are stated to be public, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central generation comparison is not fully fair: PrITTI is conditioned on vegetation-density labels, while the baseline models are unconditional. This conditioning difference confounds the reported Precision/Recall/FID improvements, and no unconditional PrITTI variant is evaluated.

Downstream editability and controllability claims are largely supported only by qualitative examples. Inpainting, outpainting, and object-level editing are not quantitatively evaluated, and there is no user study; the abstract/introduction overclaim what the experiments establish.

Reconstruction results are not competitive with the strongest baselines: Table 1 reports PrITTI at 70.27 mIoU, versus XCube at 79.47 and SemCity-1M at 93.81. Even accounting for voxelization disadvantage, the claim of comparable reconstruction quality is weak.

The photo-realistic street-view synthesis uses an off-the-shelf ControlNet model; this is not a core methodological contribution, and it is not quantitatively evaluated. It should not be used to support the paper's main claims about generation capability.

The primitive representation is coarse: objects are limited to cuboids/ellipsoids and ground surfaces are fixed-resolution 2D raster maps. The authors acknowledge failures on thin structures such as lamps and fences, but these limitations materially restrict real-world fidelity.

Controllability is demonstrated only for vegetation-density labels. The paper does not show control over object categories, object attributes, or more complex layout constraints, despite using broad terms such as controllable and editable.
The experimental scope is limited to KITTI-360. There is no cross-dataset evaluation, leaving generalization to other urban datasets or domains unverified.

Several technical details, including some loss formulations and dataset preprocessing choices, are relegated to the supplementary material. While acceptable, the main paper alone does not fully justify all design choices or allow complete assessment of robustness.
